name: Inspection minutes that cover every job
brief:
A safety inspector walks a factory at whole minutes she chooses, at most once in each minute. Each job `[start, end, need]` runs from minute `start` to minute `end`, both included, and must be seen at `need` different minutes while it runs. One visit counts for every job running at that minute.

Write `fewest_checks(jobs)`, which returns the fewest visits that give every job its `need`.

Example. For `jobs = [[1, 4, 2], [3, 6, 2], [6, 8, 1]]`, visits at minutes 3, 4 and 6 work: the first job sees 3 and 4, the second sees 3, 4 and 6, and the third sees 6. Two visits cannot serve all three jobs, so the answer is 3.
constraints: At most $10{,}000$ jobs, with $0 \le$ `start` $\le$ `end` $\le 10^9$ and $1 \le$ `need` $\le 5$; a job is never asked for more minutes than it runs.
Sorting the jobs and placing each visit with a binary search is the target; trying sets of minutes is far too slow.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Take the jobs by end time. Count the visits already inside the current job, and place any that are missing as late as possible: at `end`, then `end - 1`, skipping minutes already used. A late visit serves the most jobs still to come.

examples.note: Minutes 3 and 4 serve the first two jobs, and minute 6 serves the last two.
The first job needs all three of its minutes, and minute 1 serves the second as well.

tests.call: fewest_checks([[i, i + 9, 5] for i in range(0, 100000, 10)])

how: Submit runs 15 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value. The obvious method tries sets of minutes, which doubles with every minute; the step to the target is to take jobs by end and place each missing visit as late as it will go. The change from covering each job once is the count `need`, so each job is checked for how many visits it already holds, and new visits must skip minutes already used.
notes: Taken by end, the latest free minutes of a job serve every later job at least as well as any other minutes inside it.
Visits already inside a job count towards its need, and a new visit can never reuse a minute.
The sort costs $O(n \log n)$, and each visit costs a binary search and an insert near the end of the sorted list.

planted.slip: Placing new visits from the start of a job wastes them on minutes later jobs cannot use.
Adding visits at the end minutes without checking which are used counts the same minute twice.
Adding visits only to a job that has none treats one visit as enough for a job that needs more.
Keeping the visits in the order placed and counting only the last five for each job counts visits inside the job that sit earlier in the list, and misses others.
Trying every set of minutes by size is right but doubles with every minute, far too slow when the jobs span many minutes.
